report:
**Conclusion: probably yes, but the certainty is limited.** Monk’s pepper (also called chasteberry or *Vitex agnus-castus*) can reduce PMS symptoms for some people, so a categorical “no” is not supported by the available research.

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis specifically assessed randomized trials of *Vitex* for PMS/PMDD, indicating that there is a clinical-trial evidence base rather than only traditional use. Its existence does not establish a large or certain benefit, however: formulations, doses, PMS definitions, and symptom measures differ between studies, which limits how confidently results can be generalized.  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-psychiatry/article/treatment-of-premenstrual-syndrome-with-preparations-of-vitex-agnus-castus-chasteberry-a-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/C11517A1EF3D285632F73F23E32F0FE2

The counterpoint is important: the Cochrane record is a **withdrawn protocol**, not a completed Cochrane review confirming effectiveness. Thus, one should not portray the evidence as definitive or as equivalent to a strong guideline-backed treatment.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004632.pub2/information

Safety is also relevant. NCCIH says chasteberry appears generally well tolerated short-term; extracts have been used in research for up to three months. But pregnancy or breastfeeding may be unsafe, and people taking medicines—especially treatments affecting hormones or dopamine—should ask a clinician or pharmacist before use.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chasteberry

**Bottom line:** It is reasonable to say monk’s pepper *may* improve PMS symptoms, but not that it reliably works for everyone. It should not replace evaluation for severe PMS/PMDD or other causes of cyclical symptoms.
